name: Felix Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential and is never traced back to you. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm an employment lawyer at Hartwell & Crane, a mid-sized firm, and most of my clients are small and medium businesses with a staff problem. A normal day is a dismissal that's gone wrong, a contract that needs rewriting, and two or three phone calls with stressed managers. I cycle in along the canal, I'm at my desk by half past eight, and the first hour is usually drafting with an AI tool open beside me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone calls more than I expected, when a shop owner rings in a panic and I can tell them it's fixable. What wears me out is billing: logging every six minutes of my day on a timesheet. I'm also the one everybody asks when the AI tool does something odd, which is flattering but eats my afternoons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's roughly where I'd have bet two years ago. It would make my life calmer, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently, to the partners who wanted to buy every new product. Online I'd probably post that the tools are useful assistants, not lawyers, so let's stop pretending. At work I'd say we should keep the two tools that actually save time and cancel the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've put a lot of evenings into learning this stuff. My edge at the firm is partly that I'm the AI person, and in this world that edge is smaller. But my job is safe, my pay goes up on the normal ladder, and I'd stop worrying about junior lawyers being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing employment work and aim for senior associate in about three years. I'd keep my drafting templates, because they really do save me an hour a day on settlement agreements. And I'd move the money I've been keeping as a just-in-case fund into a flat deposit, maybe 15,000 over two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, with a small sting of having backed the wrong horse. It feels like a normal career again, which I'd take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge shrinks. Who at work gains from that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Ruth Gallagher, my supervising partner, who never trusted any of it and does everything by phone and handshake. She'd be proved right, and the firm would value relationships over speed again. If AI turns out to be hype, the partner who never opened the tools wins, and I'm just the guy who knows some shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hour a day the templates save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now that hour goes straight back into billable work, honestly. In this world I'd try to keep some of it for finding clients, like running free lunchtime talks for local HR managers. That's where new work comes from, and a talk is something a tool can't give for me.

say: I'd tell the partners the tools are **useful assistants**, not lawyers, and we should stop overpaying.
I'd suggest keeping the **two tools** that save time and cancelling the rest.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed**, because my evenings learning AI become a smaller edge.
My **job and pay** stay safe, and the worry about junior lawyers being replaced goes away.
do: Aim for **senior associate** in about three years on the normal ladder.
Keep his **drafting templates**, which save about an hour a day on settlement agreements.
Put about **15,000 over two years** towards a flat deposit.
feel: **Relieved** to have a normal career again, with a small **sting** of backing the wrong horse.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, the partner who never opened the tools wins, and I'm just the guy who knows some shortcuts.
fieldNote: Felix's identity at work is partly being **the AI person**, so a plateau costs him status, not income.
He names his partner **Ruth Gallagher** as the winner, without any bitterness.
Money talk turns quickly to a **flat deposit**, showing his savings feel secure here.

steps.text: Keep doing employment work and aim for senior associate in three years
Save about 15,000 over two years for a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels like what's already starting at our firm, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance: a firm that uses AI well can sell fixed-fee packages that small businesses can actually afford. I'd pitch that to the partners in a proper written proposal. Online I'd be the annoying optimist, posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know a lot of what I bill for is exactly the writing and checking on that card. The first thing to go is the junior work, like research memos, and then the middle, which is me. I'm the guy who taught the firm to use AI, and I've basically written the training manual for whoever replaces me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who designs the fixed-fee products, not the person who drafts each letter. In the first year I'd ask Ruth, my supervising partner, for one day a week to build an employment-law help package for small firms. I'd also put 300 a month extra into savings, because if the firm cuts a layer, I want six months of expenses, not four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit sick, both at the same time. Like standing at the top of a ski run I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, the trainee I eat lunch with, because trainees are where firms save money first. She's sharp, but her whole first two years are research and first drafts. I'd tell her to get into hearings and in front of clients as much as she can, as early as she can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners say no to your proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look elsewhere within six months, honestly. There are a few legal-tech companies and two bigger firms nearby hiring people who understand both law and the tools. I'd rather move on my own terms than wait for a restructuring letter.

say: I'd pitch AI-powered **fixed-fee packages** that small businesses can actually afford.
Online I'd be the **optimist**, posting about how firms can use the change.
think: The writing and checking I **bill for** is exactly what the card says AI takes.
Trainees go first, then the **middle layer**, which is me.
do: Ask his supervising partner for **one day a week** to build a small-business help package.
Save **300 a month** extra to reach six months of expenses.
Look at **legal-tech firms** and bigger firms within six months if the pitch fails.
feel: **Excited** and a bit **sick** at once, like the top of an unfamiliar ski run.
S1.quote: I'm the guy who taught the firm to use AI, and I've basically written the training manual for whoever replaces me.
fieldNote: Felix sees his own skill as the thing that **trains his replacement**, and says so plainly.
His first worry is for **Priya**, the trainee, rather than himself.
He sets a **six-month deadline** for moving, which fits his comfort with risk.

steps.text: Ask Ruth for a day a week to build a fixed-fee help package
Put an extra 300 a month into savings
Apply to legal-tech firms if the partners turn him down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's basically before my next promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say the law still needs a human to take responsibility, sign things and stand up in a tribunal. I'd say clients will always want someone to blame. I'd believe about half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my work is almost all thinking work: reading, writing, advising. The robots don't matter to me, it's 2028 for my whole job. By 2028 a small bakery could get better employment advice from a chatbot for free than I give for 250 an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop thinking about senior associate and think about what's left when advice is free. I'd move toward tribunal advocacy, because standing up in a hearing room still needs a person for a while, and I'd do the advocacy course this spring. I'd drop the flat plan, keep my savings in cash, and talk to my flatmate Tobi about moving somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly, for the first time. My chest gets tight just saying 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come about three years later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing good for me personally, because there's nothing hands-on in my job except carrying files. It does make me think of my dad's old idea that I should have learned a trade. Three years of electricians being safe while lawyers aren't is a funny reversal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat deposit plan goes first, then the gym and the ski trip. I've got about four months of expenses saved, which feels like a lot until you picture the whole profession looking for work in the same year.

say: I'd argue the law still needs a **human to take responsibility** and sign things.
I'd say clients will always want **someone to blame**, though I'd only half believe it.
think: My job is almost all **thinking work**, so 2028 hits all of it at once.
Free AI advice could beat what I charge at **250 an hour**.
do: Take a **tribunal advocacy** course this spring and push towards hearings.
Drop the **flat deposit** plan and cancel the gym and ski trip.
Talk to his flatmate about **moving somewhere cheaper**.
feel: **Properly scared** for the first time, with a **tight chest** at 2028.
S2.quote: By 2028 a small bakery could get better employment advice from a chatbot for free than I give for 250 an hour.
fieldNote: The optimist of the slower picture turns **sharply worried** once the date is two years away.
He sees **no robot gap** for himself, since his work has nothing hands-on.
Four months of savings feels thin because **the whole profession** would be job hunting together.

steps.text: Take a tribunal advocacy course this spring
Drop the flat deposit and cancel the gym and ski trip
Look with his flatmate Tobi for a cheaper flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit of air. Not much, but some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms have five years to rethink what a lawyer is for, and ours should start this year. I'd say it in the partners' meeting, which I'd normally be too junior to speak at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could make senior associate and then watch the role disappear under me. Thinking work goes in 2031 and my job is all thinking work, so the real question is what I'm doing on the day it lands. Five years is long enough to build something, and short enough that I can't waste one of them hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to learn the technical side properly, maybe a part-time course in legal technology, while still billing. By year three I'd want to be working for a company that builds these tools, helping them get the employment law right. And I'd save hard, aiming for a full year of expenses by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but focused. It's the kind of fear I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep billing for two years. Isn't that hedging?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is, and on purpose. I need the salary and the title to be taken seriously when I jump. Leaving with nothing lined up because a chart scared me would be silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya, the trainee, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to treat her training contract as a ticket, not a career. Get qualified, then pick something with people in the room, like tribunal work or mediation, where somebody still has to sit across from a scared manager.

say: Firms have **five years** to rethink what a lawyer is for.
I'd speak up in the **partners' meeting**, even though I'm normally too junior.
think: I could make senior associate and then **watch the role disappear** under me.
Five years is enough to **build something** but not enough to waste one hoping.
do: Take a **part-time course** in legal technology while still billing for two years.
Aim to join a company that **builds legal AI** by year three.
Save towards **a full year** of expenses by 2030.
feel: **Tense but focused**, with a fear he can actually act on.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build something, and short enough that I can't waste one of them hoping.
fieldNote: Felix admits his two-year **hedge** is deliberate, to keep the title for his next move.
His advice to Priya, **training as a ticket**, mirrors his own plan.
Five years moves him from fear to **planning**, unlike the two-year picture.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time legal technology course next year
Move to a company building legal AI by year three
Save towards a full year of expenses by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That changes the maths a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for the profession to adapt, and that law schools should start teaching it now. I'd probably volunteer to give a talk at my old university about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years almost makes me relaxed, which might be a mistake. I'd have time to get senior, save properly and then switch while I'm still young enough to start again. At 37 I can still start over, but I'd rather start over with ten years of savings than with four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the normal ladder for five years, but save a third of every pay rise rather than spend it. Around year five I'd move into mediation or another role where I'm the human face of the advice. I'd also buy a small flat after all, because a mortgage paid down by 2036 is a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but manageable. It's a cloud on the horizon, not a storm overhead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is when people often think about children too. Does that come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, actually, though I'm single at the moment. I'd want to be on solid ground before any of that, so this pushes me to sort the career out first. It's strange to plan your love life around a technology date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robot part comes around 2039. Does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for my work, but for what I'd move into, yes. If I pick something done in person, I'd get a bit of extra time, which is why mediation in the room appeals. I don't think I'd ever learn to rewire a house, though.

say: A **decade** is enough time for the profession to adapt.
Law schools should start **teaching it now**, and I'd give a talk at my old university.
think: Ten years almost makes me **relaxed**, which might be a mistake.
I'd rather start over at 37 with **real savings** than with four months.
do: Save **a third** of every pay rise for the next five years.
Move into **mediation** or a client-facing role around year five.
Buy a **small flat** and pay the mortgage down before 2036.
feel: **Uneasy but manageable**, like a cloud on the horizon rather than a storm overhead.
S4.quote: At 37 I can still start over, but I'd rather start over with ten years of savings than with four months.
fieldNote: The ten-year window brings back the **normal ladder**, with a planned exit at year five.
He links the timeline to **family plans** himself, then laughs at it.
He looks for **in-person work** to gain some of the robot gap.

steps.text: Save a third of every pay rise for five years
Move into in-person mediation around year five
Buy a small flat and pay the mortgage down early

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to turn around and my whole job is thinking work. What would help is a firm, or a government scheme, that pays for retraining while you're still employed, not after. I can retrain fast, but nobody can retrain fast with rent due and no salary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who decides how fast it goes. It's not lawyers like me, it's whoever buys the tools, and the partners at my firm will buy whatever cuts costs. I'd like someone to ask clients what they actually want from a lawyer.

headlineQuote: I can retrain fast, but nobody can retrain fast with rent due and no salary.
portrait: Felix Bauer is a 27-year-old **employment lawyer** at a mid-sized firm, advising small businesses on staff problems.
He's the firm's **AI person**, using tools daily, and sees that edge as both strength and risk.
In the slower pictures he plans to **pitch new products** or move to legal tech on his own terms.
AGI by 2028 shakes him most, because his job is **all thinking work** with no robot gap.
With **ten years**, he relaxes into saving hard and moving towards in-person mediation.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to turn around and his whole job is thinking work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while still employed, from the firm or the government, not after the salary stops.
